papers.title: Oral microbiome and DNA virome profiling in pigs reveals age-associated dynamics and extracellular recovery of Streptococcus suis-associated phage lineages
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.21.768310 v1

summary.one_liner: Shotgun metagenomic profiling of oral fluids from pigs on 15 Irish farms, using paired bulk and virus-like-particle enrichment, maps age-linked succession of oral bacteria and DNA phages and identifies 26 predicted phages targeting Streptococcus suis.
summary.plain: Researchers sampled the saliva-like oral fluid of pigs at different ages on commercial farms and sequenced all the genetic material in it, both the bacteria and the viruses that infect them. The microbial and viral communities shifted in a fairly predictable way as the pigs aged, especially after weaning. Among tens of thousands of viral groups found, 26 were predicted to infect Streptococcus suis, a pig pathogen.
summary.why: Pig oral microbes and viruses are relevant to herd health and to transmission of disease, and the paper offers a first catalogue of phages that may infect S. suis, which could inform phage-based or microbiome-targeted approaches. Whether these phages are useful as treatments is not shown here; the text only describes predicted targets from sequence data.
summary.background:
- Metagenomics: sequencing all DNA in a sample at once, then matching fragments to known organisms.
- Virome: the set of viruses in a sample; here, DNA viruses only.
- Bacteriophage (phage): a virus that infects bacteria.
- VLP (virus-like particle) enrichment: a lab step that concentrates viral particles so viral DNA is better represented.
- vOTU (viral operational taxonomic unit): a cluster of similar viral sequences treated as one viral "species".
- Streptococcus suis: a bacterium that causes disease in pigs and can occasionally infect people.
- Weaning: the point when piglets stop nursing and switch to solid feed, a major dietary change.
- Resistome: the collection of antibiotic resistance genes in a sample.

papers.abstract: The pig oral cavity is a critical interface for microbial transmission and herd health monitoring, yet its microbiome and virome remains poorly characterised. We performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing of oral fluids from pigs across 15 commercial farms in Ireland, using paired bulk and virus-like particles (VLP) enrichment to capture comprehensive microbial and DNA virome diversity. Microbial communities shifted progressively with age, with early post-weaning animals enriched in environmental genera such as Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus and later stages dominated by lactic acid bacteria and anaerobes. Only 20.6% of vOTUs could be assigned to a known genus, with the most abundant being Astrithrvirus, which increased with age. Both microbiome and DNA virome exhibited predictable, coordinated age-associated succession with strong cross-domain coupling supported by virus-host networks. Functional profiling of the microbiome revealed that predicted carbohydrate substrates tracked the dietary transitions, while accessory viral functions partitioned by lifestyle and host. The early post-weaning stage was characterised by high abundance of viral integration and excision functions, as well as elevated resistome diversity that was almost exclusively of prokaryotic origin rather than viral. Importantly, 26 of the 25,223 vOTUs identified were predicted to target Streptococcus suis, providing the first metagenomic catalogue of such phages from pig oral environments. These findings expand our understanding of oral microbiome-virome dynamics and establish a framework for integrated microbiome and viromics approaches that could enable therapeutic phage discovery and inform microbiome-targeted interventions in pig production systems.

papers.title: Infant formula composition is linked to distinct patterns of early gut colonization
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768025 v1

summary.one_liner: In 240 exclusively formula-fed infants in the Lifelines-NEXT cohort, reconstructed nutrient profiles of 17 formulas (62 components) were linked to species richness and to species-level gut colonization, with higher iron tied to lower Bifidobacterium breve and B. bifidum and higher Clostridium paraputrificum, supported by in vitro iron-limitation growth assays on stool isolates.
summary.plain: Babies who are fed infant formula receive different formulas, and the amounts of nutrients in them vary. This study asked whether those differences change which bacteria settle in the baby's gut during the first three months. The researchers reconstructed the nutrient content of the 17 formulas used by 240 infants and compared it with the gut bacteria found in each infant.
summary.why: Formula is a common early diet, so knowing that its nutrient levels relate to gut bacteria could eventually inform how formulas are designed or chosen. The text shows associations and lab growth tests only; it does not show that changing formula iron or other nutrients would change infant health, so the practical link is still unproven.
summary.background:
- Gut microbiota: the community of bacteria living in the intestine; early colonization is when these communities first establish.
- Infant formula: manufactured milk substitute whose nutrient content (vitamins, minerals, iron, etc.) can differ between brands.
- Birth cohort: a study that follows a group of people from birth to track exposures and outcomes.
- Species richness: how many different bacterial species are present.
- Bifidobacterium and Clostridium: genera of gut bacteria; Bifidobacterium species are commonly associated with infant guts.
- Association vs. causation: the study finds statistical links between formula components and bacteria, which do not by themselves prove cause.
- In vitro growth assay: testing how bacteria grow in a lab dish under set conditions, here limited iron.

papers.abstract: Early-life nutrition shapes the gut microbiota and can have long-term health implications. While infant formula feeding is widespread, it remains unclear how variations in its nutritional components shape microbiome colonization. Here, we reconstructed 62 components across the 17 infant formulas consumed during the first three months of life in 240 exclusively formula-fed infants in the Lifelines-NEXT birth cohort. Formula composition varied widely and several micronutrients, including vitamin E and iodine, were associated with species richness. Components were also associated with species-level colonization patterns. Higher iron content was associated with reduced Bifidobacterium breve and Bifidobacterium bifidum and increased Clostridium paraputrificum. Follow-up in vitro growth assays on infant-derived stool isolates showed that Bifidobacterium breve and Bifidobacterium bifidum tolerated iron limitation, while C. paraputrificum did not, consistent with the association signals. These findings show that infant formulas are not all alike and differences in component concentration affect microbiome colonization in early-life.

papers.title: Intradermal and intranasal vaccination with microparticulated ASFV proteins induces distinct immune profiles in pigs
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.768517 v1

summary.background:
- African swine fever (ASF) is a severe viral disease of pigs with large economic impact on the pig industry.
- Live attenuated vaccines (weakened live virus) work but raise biosafety concerns, so subunit vaccines (made from selected viral parts) are being explored.
- Vaccines can be given by different routes (intradermal = into the skin; intranasal = into the nose), which can shape the immune response.
- Two main immune arms: antibodies (proteins that b
summary.one_liner: In pigs, intradermal and intranasal vaccination with the same nanoparticle-delivered ASFV protein cocktail produced distinct immune profiles, but no group was protected against a virulent challenge.
summary.plain: African swine fever is a deadly virus that infects pigs and has no safe, widely approved vaccine. This study tested whether giving the same set of viral proteins by different routes, under the skin or into the nose, changes the kind of immune response pigs make. Skin injection produced antibodies in the blood but only modest cell-based immunity, while nasal delivery alone produced no detectable blood antibodies or cell responses before challenge.
summary.why: Vaccine research for this disease is limited by safety concerns with live vaccines, so comparing delivery routes helps show which immune responses matter. The authors report that antibodies alone did not protect, which supports the view that cell-mediated immunity is important; the text does not establish how this would translate to field vaccines.

papers.abstract: African Swine Fever (ASF) is a major threat to the swine industry due to its severe socioeconomic impact and the lack of safe and effective vaccines. Although live attenuated vaccines (LAVs) can induce robust immunity, biosafety concerns restrict their use, making subunit vaccines the preferred alternative. In this context, understanding how vaccination routes modulate immunity is critical. A previous study using a viral vector-based vaccine, encoding for the ASFV antigens p30, p54, p72, p72c and CD2v, induced protection when combining intranasal (IN) and parenteral administrations. However, the relative contribution of each administration route to vaccine-induced immunity remains unclear. Here we investigated how independent and combined vaccination routes influence the immune responses induced by the same ASFV protein cocktail delivered as nanoparticle-based secretory granules. Following a prime-boost regime, pigs vaccinated via intradermal (ID) route seroconverted and developed strong systemic ASFV-specific IgG responses, despite inducing only modest ASFV-specific cellular responses. In contrast, IN administration alone failed to elicit detectable systemic humoral or cellular responses and did not improve the vaccine-induced immunogenicity when combined with the ID route. Following a challenge with a virulent ASFV strain, no protection was achieved in any of the immunized groups. Interestingly, intranasally vaccinated pigs exhibited an accelerated post-challenge ASFV-specific antibody boost in serum compared to controls, suggesting that vaccination through this mucosal route induced immune priming despite the absence of detectable systemic humoral responses before challenge. Overall, these findings reveal distinct route-dependent immune profiles elicited by the same ASFV antigen cocktail and highlight again that robust humoral responses alone are insufficient for protection, further supporting the importance of cellular immunity in vaccine-induced protection.

papers.title: A multi-scale forecasting framework to prioritize clinically-relevant antibiotic resistance alleles
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768016 v1

summary.background:
- Antibiotic resistance: bacteria evolve changes that let them survive drugs that would normally kill them.
- Allele: a variant form of a gene; here, a specific DNA change in a gene.
- gyrA: a bacterial gene for an enzyme (DNA gyrase) that fluoroquinolone antibiotics like ciprofloxacin target.
- S81L: a specific single amino-acid change at position 81 of the GyrA protein, swapping serine for leucine.
- Nucleotide substitution likelihood: how readily a given DNA letter change happens by chance.
- Pharmacokinetics: how the body absorbs, distributes and clears a drug over time, which sets how drug levels fluctuate.
- Stochastic modeling: simulation that includes random chance in births, deaths and mutations.
- Virtual twin cohort: a simulated group of patients with varied characteristics, used to test scenarios.
summary.one_liner: A computational framework combining mutation likelihoods, continuous-time stochastic modeling and population pharmacokinetics that prioritizes clinically common fluoroquinolone-resistance alleles (gyrA S81L) in Acinetobacter baumannii, with virtual-twin cohort simulations of drug penetration and immunity.
summary.plain: Bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics through specific genetic changes, but lab tests do not always predict which changes will spread once a drug is widely used. This paper builds a computer model that combines how likely each DNA change is to occur with how drug levels rise and fall in patients. Using the antibiotic ciprofloxacin and the bacterium Acinetobacter baumannii as a test case, the model ranks the common gyrA mutation S81L above rarer ones, matching what is seen in hospitals.
summary.why: Antibiotic resistance is a major global health threat, and better ways to anticipate which resistance mutations will take hold could inform drug development and risk checks. The authors also report limits: the same approach did not explain success in the pmrB and adeS genes, so it is a proof of concept rather than a general predictor.

papers.abstract: Established in vitro measures for the emergence of antimicrobial resistance, a critical global threat, can fail to predict which in vitro discovered mutations will dominate in the real world following widespread antibiotic use. Here, we introduce a multi-scale computational framework integrating genetic constraints and population pharmacokinetics and apply it to explain resistance allele success in Acinetobacter baumannii for the historic case of resistance to the fluoroquinolone antibiotic ciprofloxacin. By coupling intrinsic nucleotide substitution likelihoods with continuous-time stochastic modeling under fluctuating drug exposures, our framework clearly prioritizes the most common real world gyrA fluoroquinolone resistance allele S81L over rarer alleles, reflecting its clinical success. While gyrA serves as a proof-of-concept case study for direct, active-site drug-target interactions where the target space is constrained, we observe that the nucleotide substitution likelihoods are not explaining allele success in resistance-determining genes pmrB and adeS. Furthermore, "virtual twin" cohort simulations reveal that restricted drug penetration or compromised immunity expands selective windows, rescuing rare, low-fitness alleles. This advances our understanding of prospective, model-informed risk prediction during antibiotic development.

papers.title: Local macrophage and cDC1 cooperation in the liver drives T-cell immune surveillance against pioneering metastatic cancer cells.
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.21.768283 v1

summary.background:
- Metastasis: cancer cells leaving a tumor and seeding new growth elsewhere, here in the liver.
- Intravital imaging: filming living cells inside an intact animal organ with microscopes.
- Kupffer cells: macrophages (immune cells that engulf material) resident in the liver.
- Dendritic cells (cDC1): immune cells that capture antigens (molecular pieces of a pathogen or tumor) and present them to T cells; cross-presentation means displaying material from outside the cell.
- T cells: immune cells that can kill targeted cells once activated.
- Flt3L-Ig: a drug used in mice to expand dendritic cell populations.
summary.one_liner: Intravital imaging of early liver metastasis in mice shows that resident Kupffer cells, macrophages and cDC1 dendritic cells cooperate via antigen cross-presentation to recruit T cells into activation clusters that help control arriving tumor cells.
summary.plain: Cancer often spreads to the liver through the bloodstream, and this study asks how the liver's own immune cells respond when the first tumor cells arrive. Using live imaging inside the organ, the authors describe three stages: routine immune patrolling, a rush of neutrophils and macrophage uptake of tumor material, and T-cell activation in small clusters within the liver. Boosting dendritic cell numbers with Flt3L-Ig reduced successful metastasis in their experiments.
summary.why: It maps the earliest immune steps against metastasis in a major target organ, which may matter for designing therapies that prime local immunity. The text does not show whether these mouse findings translate to human patients, so that link remains open.

papers.abstract: The liver is one of the most frequent sites for hematogenous metastasis across different types of cancer, but how the liver mounts effective immune responses against arriving tumor cells is not fully understood. Using intravital imaging, we have visualized the initial steps of liver metastasis and delineated three phases in the immune response at the earliest stages of liver metastasis: first, there is continuous surveillance of the liver parenchyma by discrete immune cell subsets in the premetastatic tissue. Second, upon metastatic cell arrival, there is massive neutrophil recruitment and tumor-cell material uptake mediated by resident macrophages. Third, antitumor-specific T-cell activation takes place in situ within intrahepatic leukocyte clusters. We find that tumor-derived material uptake triggers transcriptional programs in liver myeloid cells that upregulate chemoattraction programs in Kupffer cells and cDCs, leading to T-cell activation. Antigen cross-presentation and a functional partnership between cDC1s and local macrophages to recruit and form T-cell activation clusters are required for the elicitation of these intrahepatic T-cell responses. Consequently, prior expansion of cDCs by Flt3L-Ig treatment significantly enhances immunosurveillance, curtailing successful metastasis development. Collectively, our findings identify coordinated immune responses that are essential for anti-metastatic immunity within the liver, uncovering a program to mount defenses against tumor cells arriving in the liver.

papers.title: Viral genetic variation programs divergent neuroimmune states during rabies infection
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768130 v1

summary.background:
- Rabies virus (RABV) spreads through the nervous system and is nearly always fatal once symptoms appear.
- Field strains are viruses taken from wild or domestic animals; attenuated strains are weakened versions, often used as a basis for vaccines.
- Interferons are signalling proteins that alarm cells and trigger antiviral defences; some viruses carry proteins (here, the phosphoprotein) that block this alarm.
- Complement is a group of blood and tissue proteins that help clear pathogens and can also drive inflammation.
- Proteomics measures the proteins present in tissue; spatial imaging shows where in the tissue they are found.
- Recombinant viruses are built in the lab with specific genetic changes to test what each change does.
summary.one_liner: In mice infected intracerebrally with genetically distinct rabies viruses, temporal proteomics and spatial imaging show that viral genetics, through interferon antagonism, shape divergent brain immune states that are not simply proportional to viral load.
summary.plain: Rabies is a virus that attacks the brain, and different strains can cause very different immune reactions even when they reach similar levels in the tissue. The researchers infected mice directly into the brain with several engineered rabies viruses, including disease-causing field strains, a weakened strain, and a new variant that is more sensitive to interferon, an antiviral alarm signal. They then tracked protein changes over time and mapped where immune cells appeared in different brain regions.
summary.why: The text suggests that how much virus is present does not fully predict the strength or type of the host's immune response, which matters for understanding why some infections trigger brain inflammation and others do not. The work is limited to mice and a direct brain-injection model, so any link to human rabies or to vaccine design is an open question the text does not settle.

papers.abstract: Viral burden does not necessarily predict the extent or composition of the host immune response, reflecting the complexity of virus - host interactions. Rabies virus (RABV) provides a powerful model to investigate this question because genetically distinct RABVs differ in replication, immune evasion, and neuroimmune activation. Here, we performed integrated temporal proteomic and spatial imaging analyses of recombinant RABV, including pathogenic, attenuated, and a newly generated interferon-sensitive variant with disrupted phosphoprotein antagonistic activity. Following intracerebral infection of mice, viruses established distinct neuroimmune states that diverged over time in antiviral signaling, complement activation, and immune response. Notably, the pathogenic field viruses rDogA and rFox both exhibited substantial viral accumulation, but elicited markedly different central nervous system (CNS) responses, with rDogA inducing limited host immune engagement, whereas rFox triggered early and broad antiviral, complement, and immune recruitment programs. Disruption of phosphoprotein-mediated interferon antagonism in rDogA enhanced interferon-stimulated gene expression and antiviral effectors, restricting viral accumulation without inducing broad neuroimmune remodeling. Conversely, the attenuated glycoprotein-modified rSAD GASGAS elicited strong complement activation and T cell recruitment with little detectable viral levels, revealing a highly immunogenic neuroimmune state. Spatial profiling further identified virus-dependent patterns of myeloid, astrocyte-associated, complement, and lymphocyte responses across brain regions. Together, these findings demonstrate how viral genetic background and its modulation of host antiviral responses shape divergent neuroimmune states in which viral accumulation, antiviral immunity, and CNS immune activation are differentially coordinated.

papers.title: Distinct innate immune states associate with divergent serological outcomes after syphilis treatment
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766608 v1

summary.background:
- Syphilis is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection (Treponema pallidum) treated with antibiotics.
- Nontreponemal antibody titer: a blood antibody level measured to follow treatment response; falling levels suggest cure.
- Seroreversion: antibody levels returning to normal after treatment. Serofast: antibodies remaining detectably elevated.
- Single-cell transcriptomics: measuring which genes are active in individual cells.
- Monocytes and NK (natural killer) cells: types of white blood cells involved in inflammation and killing infected or abnormal cells.
- Degranulation: NK cells releasing stored toxic granules to kill targets; a common measure of NK function.
- JNK/JUN and STAT1: intracellular signalling pathways that switch genes on; mitochondrial complex I is part of the cell's energy-producing machinery.
- HIV coinfection: many syphilis patients also carry HIV, which affects immunity.
summary.one_liner: Single-cell transcriptomics and functional assays of circulating CD14+ monocytes and NK cells across syphilis seroreversion, low- and high-titer serofast states, and HIV coinfection, linking JUN/JNK signalling and mitochondrial complex I to impaired NK degranulation.
summary.plain: Syphilis is treated with antibiotics, and blood tests for antibodies are then used to check recovery. Some patients' antibody levels drop back to normal (seroreversion), while others stay stuck at a detectable level (serofast). This study looked at two types of immune cells in the blood to see whether patients whose antibody tests look normal have fully recovered immune function, and found signs that they may not have.
summary.why: Antibody titers are the main tool for deciding whether syphilis treatment has worked, so finding immune changes that persist after antibodies normalize suggests cell-based markers could complement them. The text does not show how these findings would translate into clinical testing, so this remains a research-stage observation.

papers.abstract: The global resurgence of syphilis poses a major public health challenge, even in the era of effective antibiotic therapy. Following treatment, some patients achieve seroreversion, whereas others remain serofast with persistent nontreponemal antibody reactivity. Although nontreponemal antibody titers guide clinical follow-up, it remains unclear how closely they reflect the resolution of inflammation and recovery of immune function. We integrated single-cell transcriptomics, immunophenotyping in clinical samples, and functional assays to characterize circulating monocytes and natural killer (NK) cells across seroreversion and low- and high-titer serofast states, and further examined the impact of HIV coinfection. CD14+ monocytes retained inflammatory and CD163-associated scavenging programs after seroreversion, whereas serofast patients showed additional IFN-STAT1 activation in this subset. NK cells from serofast patients exhibited reduced JUN expression and impaired degranulation. JNK inhibition reduced the magnitude and altered the kinetics of NK cell degranulation, IFN-{gamma} production, and amphiregulin (AREG) induction. Among low-titer serofast patients, HIV coinfection was associated with higher mitochondrial complex I gene expression and partially restored NK cell degranulation compared with patients with syphilis alone. Complex I inhibition also reduced NK cell degranulation. These findings suggest that seroreversion does not necessarily indicate immune normalization and identify post-treatment immune alterations not fully captured by conventional serological monitoring, providing a rationale for investigating cellular immune markers as complementary measures of recovery after syphilis treatment.

papers.title: Homologs of the Major Vault Protein defend bacteria against ribotoxins
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768214 v1

summary.background:
- Bacteria compete with each other using toxins delivered by systems such as type VI secretion, bacteriocins, and contact-dependent inhibition.
- Ribotoxins are toxins that damage RNA; here, one cuts the anticodon loop of specific transfer RNAs (tRNAs), which are needed to read genetic code into proteins.
- A major vault protein is a component of a large, barrel-shaped particle found in eukaryotic (animal) cells whose function is still unclear.
- Band7 proteins are a family that includes this vault-related protein homolog.
- Non-coding RNA is RNA that is not translated into protein but has regulatory or structural roles.
- A transcriptional response means cells switching genes on or off in reaction to a signal.
summary.one_liner: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a band7 homolog of the major vault protein and a candidate non-coding RNA (bRNA) are required, together with the ribotoxin's target site, for defense against a tRNA-anticodon-cleaving ribotoxin, with bioinformatic evidence that these components are widespread in bacterial RNA repair systems.
summary.plain: Bacteria often fight each other with toxins that attack their cells, and this paper looks at how one bacterium, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, protects itself against toxins that chop up RNA, the molecule cells use to build proteins. The authors found that when such damage occurred, the bacterium switched on a set of repair genes, including one related to a protein found in human cells called the major vault protein. Bacteria carrying this gene were better protected against a toxin that cuts a specific tRNA, and a short non-coding RNA made from the same region was also needed.
summary.why: It offers a possible clue to the long-unexplained function of the human vault, a large cell structure, and suggests a general way bacteria may repair RNA damage caused by rivals. The text does not show how far these findings extend beyond the bacteria tested, so the link to human vaults remains a hypothesis that the authors themselves propose.

papers.abstract: Bacteria use sophisticated mechanisms to defend themselves against antibiotics and bacteriophages, yet how they combat toxins deployed during interbacterial competition remains poorly understood. Bacteria use type VI secretion, bacteriocins, and contact dependent inhibition systems to deliver antibacterial toxins that inhibit growth by antagonizing essential processes. Here, we discover that Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses homologs of the eukaryotic major vault protein and a tRNA-like noncoding RNA to defend against RNA-damaging ribotoxins. Using an engineered pyocin delivery system, we showed that P. aeruginosa sensed ribotoxin damage and activated transcription of an RNA repair operon, which included band7, a homolog of the major vault protein. Genetic analyses demonstrated that band7-expressing bacteria were significantly more protected against growth inhibition by a ribotoxin that cleaved the anticodon loop of specific tRNA. Band7 was necessary but not sufficient, and defense also required a non-coding band7 RNA (bRNA). bRNA was cleaved by the ribotoxin, suggesting a mechanism for specificity and defense. Bioinformatic analyses revealed that band7 and candidate bRNA are widely distributed within RNA repair systems across diverse bacteria. Our data suggest that bacteria use structures related to the eukaryotic vault complex to respond to RNA damage thereby providing a hypothesis for the function of the enigmatic human vault.

papers.title: Emergence of mobile fosA3-blaCTX-M-65 with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) on conjugative plasmids in avian pathogenic Escherichia coli from industrial poultry in Pakistan
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767496 v1

summary.background:
- E. coli is a common gut bacterium; avian pathogenic strains cause disease in poultry.
- Plasmids are circular, extra DNA molecules that can be copied and transferred between bacteria, carrying resistance genes.
- Conjugative plasmids can transfer themselves to other bacteria by direct contact.
- Resistance genes named here: fosA3 (fosfomycin), blaCTX-M-65 (cephalosporins such as cefotaxime), mcr-1.1 (colistin), tet(X4) (tigecycline and related tetracyclines).
- Colistin, tigecycline and fosfomycin are considered last-line or critically important drugs for human medicine.
- Hybrid assembly combines short- and long-read sequencing to reconstruct complete plasmids.
- Sequence type (ST93) is a label for a bacterial lineage; IncHI2A, IncI2, IncFIA/IncFIC are plasmid families.
summary.one_liner: Genomic study of three multidrug-resistant avian pathogenic E. coli from Pakistani broiler chickens, reporting fosA3, blaCTX-M-65, mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) co-located on conjugative plasmids (IncHI2A, IncI2, IncFIA/IncFIC).
summary.plain: Bacteria that cause disease in chickens were found carrying genes that resist several antibiotics, including last-resort drugs. The genes sit on small, mobile pieces of DNA called plasmids that can pass between bacteria. The authors sequenced the full genomes of three isolates from healthy broilers in Punjab, Pakistan, and mapped where each gene sits.
summary.why: Plasmids that carry resistance to several last-line drug classes are a concern because they can spread resistance between bacteria, including those that affect people. The paper is a small genomic case report, so it shows the combination exists in these isolates rather than how widely it has spread.

papers.abstract: The emergence of plasmid-mediated resistance to critically important antimicrobials poses a growing threat to global health. Here we report the first genomic evidence of plasmid-mediated fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 coexisting with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) in multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli from clinically healthy broiler chickens in Pakistan. Among 1,677 high-quality genomes collected through antimicrobial resistance surveillance in Punjab, Pakistan, three isolates recovered between 2022 and 2024 harboured all four resistance determinants. Hybrid genome assemblies showed that fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 were co-located on IncHI2A plasmids, whereas mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) were carried on separate IncI2 and IncFIA/IncFIC plasmids, all predicted to be conjugative; in one isolate the tet(X4) contig did not circularise. The isolates belonged to sequence type 93 and exhibited resistance to fosfomycin, colistin, tigecycline and cefotaxime. Comparative genomic analysis revealed highly conserved IncHI2A plasmid backbones, with an additional integron-associated resistance region in the 2024 isolates, suggesting acquisition of accessory resistance determinants. Resistance to three last-line antimicrobial classes and a canonical virulence profile now coexist on conjugative plasmids in poultry E. coli, a combination that favours co-selection and argues for plasmid-resolved surveillance in poultry production.

papers.title: An Infected Cryopreserved Precision-Cut Lung Slice Model for Drug Susceptibility Testing in Pneumocystis murina Pneumonia
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767844 v1

summary.background:
- Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS): very thin slices of lung tissue kept alive in culture, preserving the lung's structure and cell mix outside the body.
- Pneumocystis murina: a fungus that infects mouse lungs and is used as a model for Pneumocystis pneumonia in people.
- Dexamethasone: a steroid used here to suppress the mice's immune systems so the infection establishes.
- Cryopreservation: freezing tissue in liquid nitrogen (about -196 °C) to store it long-term.
- Viability and qPCR: viability measures how many cells are still alive; qPCR measures how much of a specific gene's RNA is present. Here, mtSSU rRNA signals fungal load and Pdpn and Sftpc are markers for lung lining cells.
- Pentamidine: an existing anti-Pneumocystis drug used as the test treatment.
summary.one_liner: The authors describe a cryopreserved mouse precision-cut lung slice model, prepared from animals with established Pneumocystis murina pneumonia, and show that pentamidine reduces fungal rRNA in thawed infected slices.
summary.plain: Pneumocystis is a fungus that causes serious pneumonia in people with weakened immune systems, and studying it usually requires live animals. This paper describes thin slices of mouse lung that were already infected in the animal, frozen for 12 days, thawed, and kept alive in the lab for testing. When the researchers treated the thawed infected slices with the drug pentamidine, the fungal genetic material dropped significantly.
summary.why: A frozen, ready-to-use lung tissue model could allow more flexible and scalable testing of anti-fungal drugs and infection biology without repeated animal work. The text reports only one drug and a single readout, so its usefulness for other pathogens or drugs is not yet shown.

papers.abstract: Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) preserve native three-dimensional lung architecture and cellular complexity, providing a valuable ex vivo platform for studying pulmonary host-pathogen interactions. However, existing PCLS infection models typically introduce microorganisms into previously uninfected tissue, while fresh PCLS prepared from infected lungs have limited experimental flexibility and scalability. To our knowledge, cryopreserved PCLS generated from lungs with an established in vivo pulmonary infection have not been described. Herein, we evaluated cryopreserved PCLS from mice with established Pneumocystis murina pneumonia (PCP) as an ex vivo platform for infection and therapeutic studies. PCLS were prepared from dexamethasone-immunosuppressed mice with established PCP, rested for 24 h, cryopreserved in a novel freezing medium for 12 days in liquid nitrogen, rapidly thawed, recovered for 24 h, and treated with pentamidine for 72 h. Viability was assessed in uninfected and PCP-infected PCLS before and after cryopreservation. Although post-thaw viability decreased in both groups, substantial viability was still retained, allowing further experimentation. qPCR showed that cryopreservation did not alter expression of the type I and type II alveolar epithelial markers podoplanin (Pdpn) and surfactant protein C (Sftpc) in either group. Importantly, pentamidine significantly reduced Pneumocystis mitochondrial small subunit (mtSSU) rRNA levels in thawed PCP-infected PCLS, demonstrating suitability for anti-Pneumocystis drug testing. These findings establish the first cryopreserved ex vivo PCP model using infected mouse PCLS, preserving endogenous fungal burden and infection-associated host responses while enabling flexible, scalable studies of Pneumocystis biology, host-pathogen interactions, therapeutic efficacy, and potentially other pulmonary infections.

papers.title: EFFECT OF A LACTOBACILLUS POSTBIOTIC ON DIGESTIVE HEALTH IN DOGS RAISED IN CONDITIONS AT RISK OF GIARDIA DUODENALIS INFECTION
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767253 v1

summary.background:
- Giardia duodenalis: a single-celled intestinal parasite that causes diarrhea in dogs and other animals.
- Metronidazole: an antibiotic/antiparasitic drug used to treat it; it can disturb beneficial gut bacteria.
- Postbiotic: a preparation of substances made by bacteria (here, Lactobacillus fermentation), not live bacteria.
- Randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled: dogs were assigned to groups by chance, and handlers or assessors did not know who got the real product versus filler.
- Microbiome and shotgun metagenomics: sequencing all DNA in stool to identify which bacteria are present and which genes they carry.
- Dysbiosis index: a score summarizing how far the gut bacterial community departs from a healthy profile.
- Calprotectin and secretory IgA: stool markers of gut inflammation and local immune defense.
summary.one_liner: A randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled trial in 30 naturally Giardia-infected Terrier dogs testing whether an adjunctive Lactobacillus-derived postbiotic (LBHF) alongside metronidazole improves parasite clearance, stool quality, and gut microbiome function.
summary.plain: Giardia is a microscopic gut parasite that causes diarrhea in dogs, and the usual antibiotic treatment, metronidazole, can further upset the gut's bacterial community. In this study, 30 infected dogs got metronidazole plus either a bacterial-derived supplement (LBHF) or a placebo filler for 21 days, and researchers tracked symptoms, parasite shedding, and gut bacteria over 45 days. The supplement group had lower parasite levels during treatment, firmer stools, and less odor, but other gut and blood markers did not differ.
summary.why: Giardia is common in dogs and treatment can be hard to get right, so a low-cost adjunct that speeds recovery would matter if it holds up. The paper only reports associations and says mechanistic studies are still needed, so the link between the observed microbiome changes and parasite clearance is unproven.

papers.abstract: Giardia duodenalis infection is associated with diarrhea and dysbiosis in dogs, while metronidazole treatment can further disrupt the microbiota. We evaluated adjunctive LB fermentate HF (LBHF), a Lactobacillus-derived postbiotic, in a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled study of 30 naturally infected dogs (Terriers). Animals received metronidazole (50 mg/kg/day) with LBHF (50 mg/kg/day) or microcrystalline cellulose placebo (70 mg/kg/day) for 21 days. Clinical outcomes, fecal biomarkers, canine dysbiosis index, and cyst shedding were monitored over 45 days. Fecal shotgun metagenomics was performed at baseline and day 45. After baseline covariate adjustment, LBHF was associated with significantly lower Giardia burdens during treatment, particularly at days 10 and 20, improved fecal consistency, and reduced odor. No significant effects were found for fecal calprotectin, secretory IgA, blood biomarkers of digestive function, or canine dysbiosis index. Overall microbiome turnover was similar between groups, but multivariate analyses identified distinct treatment-associated community trajectories. LBHF was associated with increased Bacteroidota representation and functional capacity for plant polysaccharide degradation, alongside depletion of gene sets involved in flagellar assembly, quorum sensing, biofilm formation, and epithelial-cell signaling. Baseline microbiome composition also predicted Giardia burden, highlighting an association between parasite load and bacterial community structure. Adjunctive LBHF supplementation was associated with faster resolution of canine giardiasis, improved fecal quality, and coordinated microbiome remodeling. Further mechanistic studies are needed to establish whether the observed microbiome functional changes contribute to parasite clearance and recovery of intestinal health.

papers.title: Not all plant-based diets are alike: intake of minimally processed plant foods is associated with gut microbial richness among vegetarians and vegans.
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767798 v1

summary.background:
- Gut microbiome: the community of bacteria and other microbes living in the intestine.
- Species richness: how many different microbial species are present; higher is often, though not always, linked to better health.
- Shotgun metagenomics: sequencing all the DNA in a stool sample to identify which microbes are present and roughly what they carry.
- Cross-sectional study: data collected from many people at one time, so it shows correlation, not cause and effect.
- Minimally processed plant foods: foods such as whole fruits, vegetables, legumes and grains that have been little altered from their natural state.
- Standard deviation: a unit of spread in the data; the paper reports associations per one standard deviation increase in intake.
- Lacto-ovo-vegetarian: a vegetarian who eats dairy and eggs but no meat or fish.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional shotgun metagenomics study of 172 omnivorous, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and vegan adults finds that intake of minimally processed plant foods is positively associated with gut microbial species richness within the vegetarian and vegan group, but not among omnivores.
summary.plain: Diets labelled "vegetarian" or "vegan" describe only what people leave out, not what they eat or how much their food is processed. This study asked whether the amount of minimally processed plant food people eat relates to the variety of microbes in their gut. Among 172 adults, vegetarians and vegans had fewer gut species than omnivores, but within that group, those eating more minimally processed plant foods had more species.
summary.why: It suggests that a diet label alone may hide differences in gut microbes that matter for health, which could help explain mixed results on plant-based diets. The study is observational and cross-sectional, so it shows an association at one point in time and cannot establish that these foods cause the change.

papers.abstract: Plant-based diets are usually defined by what they exclude, overlooking which plant foods are eaten and how processed they are. Here we examine whether this overlooked dimension is related to the gut microbiome. In a cross-sectional study of 172 omnivorous, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and vegan adults profiled by shotgun metagenomics, vegetarians and vegans harboured fewer gut species than omnivores. Within this group, however, each standard deviation increase in minimally processed plant-food intake was associated with 27 additional species (p = 0.001), independently of fibre intake, and richness in participants with the highest intake approached that of omnivores. No such association was seen among omnivores. Higher intake was also linked to more species previously associated with favourable cardiometabolic health and to better health-related quality of life. Dietary labels alone may therefore conceal meaningful variation in the gut microbiome, and characterising how plant foods are processed may help in understanding how plant-based diets relate to health.

papers.title: Cell identity and activation state determine the innate immune response to nanoplastics
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767123 v1

summary.background:
- Nanoplastics: plastic fragments smaller than about a micrometre, which can enter the body.
- Biocorona: a layer of proteins and other molecules that sticks to a particle once it is in body fluids, changing how cells see it.
- Innate immune system: the body's fast, general-purpose defenses, including neutrophils (first responders), macrophages (cells that engulf debris and signal to others) and endothelial cells (lining of blood vessels).
- M0, M1, M2 macrophages: macrophage states; M1 is pro-inflammatory, M2 is more anti-inflammatory and tissue-repairing, M0 is resting.
- Cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6): chemical messengers that signal inflammation.
- Myeloperoxidase: an enzyme released by neutrophils that can damage tissue.
- Autoimmunity: the immune system attacking the body's own tissues.
summary.one_liner: In primary human neutrophils, macrophages and endothelial cells, biocorona-coated polystyrene nanoplastics at physiologically relevant concentrations were internalized without loss of viability but produced cell-type- and activation-state-dependent changes in innate immune function, with M1 macrophages upregulating inflammatory cytokines (including TNF-α and IL-6).
summary.plain: Tiny plastic particles, far smaller than a grain of sand, are found in the environment and may be linked to the rise in autoimmune disease, though no direct link has been shown. The researchers exposed several types of human immune and blood-vessel cells grown in the lab to these particles at levels they considered realistic. The cells took the particles up without dying, but each cell type responded differently: some released more inflammatory signals, some released fewer, and some did not change much.
summary.why: Inflammation is a key step in the onset of autoimmunity, so knowing how everyday environmental particles change immune cell behavior is relevant to public health questions. The text itself does not establish a causal link to autoimmune disease, and the work is limited to cells in the lab, so its connection to disease in people remains a hypothesis.

papers.abstract: Autoimmune disease is on the rise, and while no direct connection has been made, evidence suggests environmental toxins such as nanoplastics may be contributing to the increased incidence. A key factor in the onset of autoimmunity is inflammation; yet how nanoplastics impact innate immune function is unclear. Here, we exposed primary human neutrophils, macrophages, and endothelial cells to biocorona-coated polystyrene nanoplastics at physiologically relevant concentrations. All cells internalized nanoplastics without viability loss, but functional consequences diverged. Neutrophils increased myeloperoxidase release as nanoplastic concentration increased. Endothelial cells reduced leukocyte-recruiting mediator secretion and had decreased neutrophil adhesion following inflammatory stimulation. M1 macrophages broadly upregulated inflammatory cytokine secretion (including TNF- and IL-6), whereas M0 and M2 macrophages exhibited no significant secretory changes. Collectively, these findings indicate physiologically relevant nanoplastic concentrations do not universally increase inflammation but rather dysregulate innate immune populations in a manner that could contribute to autoimmunity.

papers.title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Methods for Antimicrobial Peptide Prediction and Discovery in Ancient Microbiomes
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767431 v1

summary.background:
- Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs): short chains of amino acids produced by organisms that can kill or inhibit bacteria, fungi, or viruses.
- Metagenomics: sequencing all DNA from a sample (such as soil or teeth) to learn which organisms and genes are present, without culturing them.
- Machine learning classifiers: computer models trained on labeled examples to predict whether a new sequence is an AMP.
- Feature configurations: different ways of describing a peptide to a model, such as its sequence, predicted 3D structure, or embeddings from protein language models (models trained on protein sequences, analogous to language models trained on text).
- Reinforcement learning: a trial-and-reward approach where a program learns to pick good candidates by receiving feedback.
- Benchmarking: a fair side-by-side comparison of methods on the same data.
- Dental calculus: hardened dental plaque that preserves microbial DNA over long periods.
summary.one_liner: A systematic benchmark of six machine learning methods and twelve feature sets for predicting antimicrobial peptides, applied to ancient metagenomes (archaeological gut sediments, dental calculus, and mammoth-associated communities) and paired with reinforcement learning for candidate selection.
summary.plain: Antimicrobial peptides are small protein fragments that can kill microbes, and they are being studied as possible alternatives to antibiotics. This paper compares many computer methods for spotting these peptides in genetic data, then uses the best ones to search DNA-derived protein sequences from ancient samples such as old gut sediments, dental tartar, and mammoth remains. The authors report that protein language model features worked best and that deep learning models outperformed older classical methods.
summary.why: Finding new antimicrobial candidates matters because antibiotic resistance is a growing problem, and the paper suggests ancient microbiomes are a largely unexplored source. The main practical value is the comparison of methods, though the candidates themselves still need laboratory testing before any claim of antimicrobial activity can be made.

papers.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics amid the growing global threat of antimicrobial resistance. Expanding AMP discovery requires both effective computational tools to accurately identify candidate peptides and access to underexplored biological resources that may harbor novel AMPs. However, the comparative performance of existing computational methods remains poorly understood, while ancient microbiomes have received limited attention as potential reservoirs of AMPs. Here, we systematically benchmarked six machine learning methods across with twelve feature configurations spanning sequence, structural, and protein language model features under a unified framework using eight curated AMP datasets. The best-performing methods were subsequently applied to three ancient metagenomic datasets representing the human gut (archaeological fecal sediments), human oral cavity (dental calculus), and mammoth-associated communities (teeth, skulls, and skin). In parallel, we employed reinforcement learning to select candidate peptides directly from ancient sequence pools without relying on modern AMP labels. Our benchmarking shows that protein language model embeddings provide the most informative features, and deep learning models, including convolutional, transformer-based, and recurrent architectures, outperform classical methods. Applying these models to ancient microbiomes identified candidates occupied the physicochemical space characteristic of AMPs but differed from those of candidates predicted from modern microbiome catalogs. We identified 111, 76, and 50 high-confidence candidate AMPs from the Neanderthal gut, ancient oral, and mammoth-associated communities, respectively. Reinforcement learning selected additional candidate AMPs with distinct properties compared with those predicted by models trained on modern AMP databases. Together, these findings establish a systematic benchmark for AMP prediction and highlight ancient microbiomes as an untapped source of antimicrobial peptide candidates. By integrating supervised machine learning with reinforcement learning, this study expands AMP discovery beyond modern microbiome catalogs and provides new opportunities to identify potentially novel AMPs.

papers.title: Seroprotection and improved polyfunctional immunity conferred by a YF17D-vectored rabies vaccine
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766779 v1

summary.background:
- Rabies is a viral disease that is almost always fatal once symptoms start; vaccination after exposure or before it is the main protection.
- Live-attenuated vaccine: a weakened but still replicating virus that triggers a strong immune response without causing disease.
- YF17D: a long-used, weakened yellow fever vaccine virus, here used as a carrier ("vector") for a rabies gene.
- Glycoprotein (RabG): the rabies virus surface protein that the immune system targets.
- Neutralizing antibodies: immune proteins that block a virus from infecting cells; their level is used as a benchmark ("correlate") of protection.
- Lyssaviruses: a genus of viruses related to rabies, including Mokola and Lagos bat viruses.
- Non-human primates, mice and hamsters: animal models used before human testing.
summary.one_liner: Preclinical study of YF-RabG, a live-attenuated yellow fever 17D vaccine vector expressing the rabies glycoprotein, reporting neutralizing antibody responses, protection in mouse challenge models, durability to one year, and adaptation to other lyssaviruses.
summary.plain: Rabies is a deadly virus, and the usual preventive shots need several doses and repeated clinic visits. This study tests a possible single-dose rabies vaccine built on a weakened yellow fever virus that carries a rabies surface protein. In animal experiments, one dose produced strong immune responses, and the authors report that it protected mice against lethal rabies and kept protective antibody levels for at least a year.
summary.why: A single-dose rabies vaccine would be useful where repeated visits are hard, and the paper also suggests the same platform could be adapted to related lyssaviruses. Whether this holds in people is not shown here; the work is in animals and would need clinical trials.

papers.abstract: Rabies remains a major public-health challenge, with pre-exposure vaccination strategies constrained by the need for multiple doses and repeated healthcare visits. Here we describe YF-RabG, a live-attenuated rabies vaccine candidate based on the yellow fever 17D (YF17D) vaccine backbone that stably expresses the rabies virus glycoprotein (RabG). YF-RabG exhibited an attenuated phenotype and favourable safety profile compared with parental YF17D across several preclinical models, including neonatal and immunocompromised mice. A single immunization induced robust humoral and cell-mediated immune responses in non-human primates. Rabies virus-neutralizing antibody titres readily exceeded the widely accepted correlate of protection in mice, hamsters and non-human primates by several orders. Accordingly, vaccination conferred protection against lethal rabies challenge in a range of stringent mouse models, maintained seroprotective antibody levels for at least one year, and increased following a boost using a licensed rabies vaccine. Furthermore, the YF17D vector was readily adapted to accommodate glycoproteins from distant lyssaviruses, generating protective vaccine candidates against Mokola, Lagos bat and Lleida bat lyssaviruses. Collectively, these findings identify YF-RabG as a promising single-dose rabies vaccine candidate and highlight the versatility of the YF17D platform for lyssavirus vaccine development.

papers.title: Spatially-Organized Adaptive Immune Niches in Granulomas Dictate Local Defense and Correlate with Disease Severity in Tuberculosis Patients
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766905 v1

summary.background:
- Granuloma: a organized ball of immune cells that forms around TB bacteria; its centre can become dead tissue (necrotic core).
- Tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS): a lymph-node-like cluster that forms in inflamed tissue, where B cells and helper T cells interact.
- Germinal center-like features: signs of B cells maturing and improving their antibodies, here linked to FCRL5-expressing antibody-producing cells.
- CD8 T cells: killer T cells; effector memory (TEM) cells are experienced cells ready to act quickly.
- Single-cell multi-omics and spatial transcriptomics: methods that measure genes in individual cells and record where in the tissue they sit.
- LGALS9: a signalling protein (galectin-9) that macrophages produce here in high amounts.
- Zebrafish: a small fish model used to study mycobacterial infection, with an lgals9 gene variant used to test the macrophage role.
- H&E staining: the standard coloured stain on pathology slides; AI here predicts gene activity from these images.
summary.one_liner: Single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics and immune receptor profiling of human tuberculosis granulomas identify two concentric adaptive immune niches (a tertiary lymphoid outer layer and a CD8 effector-memory T cell inner layer) organized by LGALS9-high macrophages, with supporting zebrafish experiments and an AI-based link to disease severity.
summary.plain: Tuberculosis forms small clusters of immune tissue called granulomas that wall off the infection. This paper maps how immune cells are arranged inside human granulomas and finds two rings around a dead central core: an outer ring that looks like a mini lymph node where B cells mature, and an inner ring of memory T cells that appear to be drawn in and expanded locally by a particular type of macrophage. Experiments in zebrafish suggest these macrophages help bring in T and B cells and limit bacterial growth.
summary.why: Granulomas are where the body fights TB, so knowing how immune cells are arranged there may help guide host-directed treatments and vaccines. The finding that predicted lymph-node-like structures rise with disease severity, inferred from routine tissue slides, could in principle be useful for clinical assessment, but the text does not show that this has been tested as a diagnostic.

papers.abstract: The cellular composition and spatial organization of immune responses within tuberculosis (TB) granulomas have been increasingly characterized, yet how these spatially organized immune cell populations coordinate local adaptive immunity remains largely unknown. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and immune receptor profiling to construct a comprehensive spatial atlas of human TB granulomas. We identified two concentric adaptive immune niches surrounding the central necrotic core. The outer niche comprised granuloma-associated tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) that supported TFH-B cell interactions and exhibited functional germinal center-like features associated with antigen-driven B-cell maturation toward FCRL5 antibody-producing cells. The inner niche contained antigen-experienced and Mtb-reactive effector memory CD8 T cells (TEM), which were recruited from distal lung regions by LGALS9high chemokine-expressing macrophages and activated to undergo local clonal expansion. In lgals9l1 deficient zebrafish, macrophage depletion was accompanied by marked reductions in T- and B-cell enrichment within granulomas and increased bacterial loads, supporting a role for LGALS9high macrophages in coordinating local adaptive immunity against TB infection. Finally, AI-based prediction of spatial gene expression from clinical hematoxylin and eosin-stained specimens revealed that inferred TLS abundance increased with TB disease severity. These findings identify spatially interconnected adaptive immune niches that organize protective immune responses within human TB granulomas, therefore providing a foundation for understanding granuloma adaptive immunity and developing host-directed therapies and vaccines for TB (https://tbomics.smart-nbc.org.cn/).

papers.title: Multivalent mRNA tuberculosis vaccines protect against mycobacterial infection in zebrafish, mice and guinea pigs
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.09.765257 v1

summary.background:
- Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which mainly infects the lungs.
- BCG is the existing TB vaccine, in use for about 100 years, and its protection is limited.
- mRNA vaccines deliver a genetic message that tells the body's cells to make a harmless piece of a pathogen, which trains the immune system.
- Antigens are the pathogen pieces the immune system learns to recognize.
- Multivalent means containing several antigens at once.
- Preclinical means tested in laboratory animals, before human trials.
- T cells are immune cells that kill infected cells and remember past threats; IFN-gamma is a signaling molecule they release.
- Zebrafish are used here as a fast screening model for finding protective antigens.
summary.one_liner: Preclinical study showing that mRNA vaccines encoding four, six, or nine Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens, selected by screening in zebrafish, reduced bacterial burden and lung pathology in mice and guinea pigs.
summary.plain: Tuberculosis is a serious infectious disease, and the only widely used vaccine, BCG, is about a century old and only partly effective. The researchers first looked for useful targets in zebrafish, then packaged several of those targets into mRNA vaccines, the same kind of technology used in some COVID-19 shots. In mice and guinea pigs, the vaccines were reported to lower the amount of bacteria and lung damage, in some cases comparably to BCG.
summary.why: Tuberculosis still causes a large share of deaths from infectious disease, so better vaccines matter. The work is preclinical (animal only), so it shows promise for the approach rather than proof that the vaccines will work in people; the abstract does not report human trial plans.

papers.abstract: Despite a century of BCG use, tuberculosis remains a leading cause of death from infectious diseases and more effective vaccines are urgently needed. Here we combined antigen discovery in zebrafish with mRNA vaccine technology to generate multivalent vaccine candidates, TUmRNA4, TUmRNA6 and TUmRNA9, encoding four, six, or nine Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens, respectively. The vaccines were well tolerated, and induced robust antigen-specific cellular immune responses, including IFN{gamma} production and expansion of memory T-cell populations. In mice, TUmRNA4 and TUmRNA6 reduced pulmonary M. tuberculosis burden and lung pathology to levels comparable to BCG vaccination and TUmRNA6 enhanced BCG-mediated protection when used as a booster vaccine. In guinea pigs, TUmRNA9 reduced bacterial burden in the lungs, spleen, and lymph nodes and decreased pulmonary lesions. These findings demonstrate that protective antigens identified in zebrafish can be translated into effective multivalent mRNA vaccines and establish a framework for tuberculosis vaccine development across multiple preclinical models.

papers.title: Synthetic diet feeding exacerbates central nervous system autoimmunity in mice independent of weight gain
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766400 v1

summary.background:
- EAE (experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis) is a mouse model of multiple sclerosis, in which the immune system attacks the brain and spinal cord.
- Synthetic (purified) diets are precisely defined lab foods, compared here with standard laboratory chow.
- Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are small molecules made by gut microbes from fiber; butyrate is one of them and is known to influence immune cells.
- T helper cells (Th17) can drive inflammation; regulatory T cells (Tregs) help calm it. Peripheral Tregs (pTregs) are Tregs made outside the thymus.
- Weight gain and high saturated fat or sugar are separate factors that the study tried to isolate from diet composition.
summary.one_liner: In mice, a synthetic purified diet independent of weight gain worsened experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), reduced systemic short-chain fatty acids, and butyrate supplementation dampened pathogenic T cell expansion and shifted the balance of peripheral Tregs to Th17 cells.
summary.plain: This study asks whether the processed, purified diets often used in lab mice can change the immune system even when the mice do not gain extra weight. In a mouse model of multiple sclerosis-like inflammation of the brain and spinal cord, mice on the synthetic diet had more severe disease, and their blood contained less of certain gut-derived fatty acids. Adding butyrate, one of those fatty acids, reduced the production of harmful immune cells and eased the disease.
summary.why: Many immunology studies compare synthetic diets against standard chow, so if diet composition alone changes disease severity, that could confound results and matters for how diet is linked to autoimmune disease. The text does not establish whether these findings apply to humans, so the link to human disease remains an open question.

papers.abstract: Consumption of a nutrient deficient diet high in saturated fats and sugar is associated with the increased incidence and exacerbation of inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. Efforts to resolve the molecular mechanisms underlying diet-dependent changes to immune responses rely on the use of synthetic diets in mice, often using a standard laboratory chow as control. Critically, it remains unknown whether synthetic diet specific alterations in nutrient and metabolite availability, independent of weight gain and exposure to dietary fats and sugar, can affect the immune response. We reveal that exposure to a synthetic diet, independent of weight gain, is sufficient to alter the immune response, driving increased severity in the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model of central nervous system (CNS) autoimmunity. Mechanistically, synthetic diet feeding leads to systemic reductions in short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) abundance, and supplementation of synthetic diet with butyrate mitigates the excessive production of pathogenic T cells, and ameliorates synthetic diet driven increases in EAE severity. Finally, we identify the presence of peripheral Tregs (pTregs) in the CNS of EAE mice, which can arise from shared clonal ancestors as T helper (Th) cells, and reveal that butyrate supplementation increases the proportion pTregs to Th17 cells during EAE.
